inlines.text: without regard to its sign, or the distance on the number line from the o

answer.worked: Absolute value measures a number's size without regard to its sign: its distance from the origin.

For a non-negative number, its absolute value is the number itself. For a negative number, changing its sign gives its distance from zero.

$$|x|=\begin{cases}x&\text{if }x\geq0,\\-x&\text{if }x<0.\end{cases}$$
The difference $x-a$ measures displacement from $a$; its absolute value measures distance from $a$.

Apply the absolute-value definition to the value $f(x)$. Keep it when it is non-negative and change its sign when it is negative.

$$|f(x)|=\begin{cases}f(x)&\text{if }f(x)\geq0,\\-f(x)&\text{if }f(x)<0.\end{cases}$$
The square root is non-negative, so $\sqrt{x^2}=|x|$ for every real $x$.
Whether $|x|=x$ or $|x|=-x$, squaring gives $|x|^2=x^2$.
The two numbers at distance $k$ from zero are $k$ and $-k$, so $x=\pm k$.

classification.difficultyReason: Complete standard symmetry, product and quotient identities and recall that the denominator must be nonzero; each part is a direct application.

answer.worked: $x$ and $-x$ are the same distance from zero, so $|-x|=|x|$.
Distance between two numbers is unchanged when their order is reversed, so $|x-y|=|y-x|$.
The magnitude of a product is the product of the magnitudes: $|xy|=|x||y|$.

The magnitude of a quotient is the quotient of the magnitudes:

$$\left|\frac{x}{y}\right|=\frac{|x|}{|y|},\qquad y\ne0.$$

The restriction excludes division by zero.

$\begin{aligned}|xy|&=|3(-5)|\\|xy|&=|-15|\\|xy|&=15\\|x||y|&=|3||-5|\\|x||y|&=3\times5\\|x||y|&=15\end{aligned}$

Both sides equal 15.

$\begin{aligned}\left|\frac{x}{y}\right|&=\left|\frac3{-5}\right|\\\left|\frac{x}{y}\right|&=\frac35\\\frac{|x|}{|y|}&=\frac{|3|}{|-5|}\\\frac{|x|}{|y|}&=\frac35\end{aligned}$

Both sides equal $\frac35$.

content.prompt:
[Solving equations using the distance definition]

Use the techniques from Question 7 to solve the following equations.

answer.worked:
The distance from 0 is 6.

$x=0\pm6=\pm6$.

$|-x|=|x|$, so $|x|=3$.

The distance from 0 is 3, giving $x=\pm3$.

$\begin{aligned}|2x|&=4\\|x|&=2\end{aligned}$

The distance from 0 is 2, giving $x=\pm2$.

The distance from $-4$ is 2.

$\begin{aligned}x&=-4\pm2\\x&=-2\text{ or }-6\end{aligned}$

The distance from 5 is 7.

$\begin{aligned}x&=5\pm7\\x&=12\text{ or }-2\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}|2x+1|&=3\\\left|x+\frac12\right|&=\frac32\end{aligned}$

The distance from $-\frac12$ is $\frac32$.

$\begin{aligned}x&=-\frac12\pm\frac32\\x&=1\text{ or }-2\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}|3-2x|&=5\\|2x-3|&=5\\\left|x-\frac32\right|&=\frac52\end{aligned}$

The distance from $\frac32$ is $\frac52$.

$\begin{aligned}x&=\frac32\pm\frac52\\x&=4\text{ or }-1\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}|3x+5|&=16\\\left|x+\frac53\right|&=\frac{16}3\end{aligned}$

The distance from $-\frac53$ is $\frac{16}3$.

$\begin{aligned}x&=-\frac53\pm\frac{16}3\\x&=\frac{11}3\text{ or }-7\end{aligned}$

classification.difficultyReason: Test f(-x) against f(x) and -f(x), using absolute-value identities; part (c) additionally requires finding the denominator restriction and recognising that an asymmetric domain rules out both parity classifications.

content.prompt: Determine whether the following functions are even, odd or neither.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}f(1)&=1+|1|=2\\f(-1)&=-1+|-1|=0\end{align*}$$
Since $f(-1)$ equals neither $f(1)$ nor $-f(1)$, the function is neither even nor odd.

$$\begin{align*}f(-x)&=(-x)|-x|\\f(-x)&=-x|x|\\f(-x)&=-f(x)\end{align*}$$
The domain is $\mathbb R$, so the function is odd.

For $x\geq0$, the denominator is $x-x=0$, so the function is undefined. For $x<0$,
$$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\frac{x}{-x-x}\\f(x)&=-\frac12.\end{align*}$$
Its domain is not symmetric about zero, so the function is neither even nor odd.

$$\begin{align*}f(-x)&=|-x-1|+|-x+1|\\f(-x)&=|x+1|+|x-1|\\f(-x)&=f(x)\end{align*}$$
The domain is $\mathbb R$, so the function is even.

content.prompt: Do you think the following statements are true or false for all values of $x$? If you think a statement is false, provide a specific value of $x$ showing this.

answer.worked:
$$|3-x|=|-(x-3)|=|x-3|.$$
An expression and its negative have the same absolute value.

At $x=2$,
$$\begin{align*}|x-1|&=|2-1|=1\\1-x&=1-2=-1.\end{align*}$$
The two sides are unequal.

$$|5x|=|5||x|=5|x|.$$
Absolute value is multiplicative.
For $x\geq0$, $|x|^2=x^2$. For $x<0$, $|x|^2=(-x)^2=x^2$. Thus the statement holds for every real $x$.

At $x=-1$,
$$\begin{align*}|-3x|&=|-3(-1)|=3\\3x&=3(-1)=-3.\end{align*}$$
The two sides are unequal.

At $x=-1$,
$$\begin{align*}\sqrt{x^2}&=\sqrt{(-1)^2}=1\\x&=-1.\end{align*}$$
The two sides are unequal. In general, $\sqrt{x^2}=|x|$.

inlines.text: Recall the following definition of the absolute value.
Use the definition to find the equations of the branches, and their respective domains, for each of the following.

answer.worked:
The argument $x-4$ is non-negative for $x\geq4$ and negative for $x<4$. Therefore
$$y=\begin{cases}x-4,&x\geq4,\\-(x-4)=-x+4,&x<4.\end{cases}$$

The argument $x+3$ is non-negative for $x\geq-3$ and negative for $x<-3$. Therefore
$$y=\begin{cases}x+3,&x\geq-3,\\-(x+3)=-x-3,&x<-3.\end{cases}$$

$$\begin{align*}2x-3&\geq0\\2x&\geq3\\x&\geq\frac32.\end{align*}$$
Thus
$$y=\begin{cases}2x-3,&x\geq\frac32,\\-(2x-3)=-2x+3,&x<\frac32.\end{cases}$$

children.prompt: Find all possible values of $a$ if $f(a)=9$.

answer.worked:
For $a\geq0$:
$$\begin{align*}9-a^2&=9,\\a^2&=0,\\a&=0.\end{align*}$$
For $a<0$:
$$\begin{align*}|a+9|&=9,\\a+9&=9\text{ or }-9,\\a&=0\text{ or }-18.\end{align*}$$
Only $-18$ belongs to the negative branch. Combining the branches gives $a=-18$ or $a=0$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find all possible values of $b$ if $f(b)=1$.

answer.worked:
For $b\geq0$:
$$\begin{align*}9-b^2&=1,\\b^2&=8,\\b&=\sqrt8=2\sqrt2.\end{align*}$$
For $b<0$:

classification.difficultyReason: Apply standard properties of y=k/x to identify axis asymptotes, excluded domain and range values, and quadrants from the sign of k.

content.prompt: For these questions, assume that $k\in\mathbb{R}$, $k\ne0$.

answer.worked: There are two asymptotes: the vertical line $x=0$ and the horizontal line $y=0$.
The branches approach the $y$-axis as $x$ approaches zero and the $x$-axis as $|x|$ increases. Thus the asymptotes are $x=0$ and $y=0$.
The denominator cannot be zero. Every other real value of $x$ is allowed, so the domain is $x\in\mathbb{R},\ x\ne0$.
Since $k\ne0$, the fraction $\dfrac{k}{x}$ cannot equal zero. Every nonzero real $y$ occurs when $x=\dfrac{k}{y}$, so the range is $y\in\mathbb{R},\ y\ne0$.
For $k>0$, $x$ and $y$ have the same sign: both positive in quadrant I and both negative in quadrant III.
For $k<0$, $x$ and $y$ have opposite signs: $x<0$, $y>0$ in quadrant II and $x>0$, $y<0$ in quadrant IV.

Initially, $y_1=\dfrac{k}{x_1}$. When $x$ is doubled,

answer.worked: Since $y_2=\dfrac{y_1}{2}$, doubling $x$ halves $y$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}y_2&=\frac{k}{x_1/2}\\y_2&=\frac{2k}{x_1}\\y_2&=2y_1.\end{align*}$$Thus $y$ doubles.
$$\begin{align*}y_2&=\frac{k}{3x_1}\\y_2&=\frac13\left(\frac{k}{x_1}\right)\\y_2&=\frac{y_1}{3}.\end{align*}$$Thus $y$ is divided by 3.

classification.difficultyReason: Explain the fixed-work inverse relationship, define variables and determine the constant product, then use the resulting model to calculate either time or workforce.

content.prompt: It takes 15 people to do a job in 20 days.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Explain briefly why this is a suitable scenario for inverse variation.

answer.short: For a fixed job, assuming equal constant work rates, more people take fewer days and fewer people take more days; the product of people and days stays constant.
answer.worked: The amount of work is fixed. Assuming each person works at the same constant rate, doubling the number of people halves the time, so the number of people multiplied by the number of days remains constant. This is inverse variation.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Assume that the relationship is inverse variation. Form an equation that models the above scenario.

answer.short: $P=\dfrac{300}{D}$, where $P$ is the number of people and $D$ is the number of days.
answer.worked:
Let $P$ be the number of people and $D$ the number of days. Inverse variation gives $P=\dfrac{k}{D}$.
$$\begin{align*}k&=PD\\k&=15\times20\\k&=300\end{align*}$$Hence $P=\dfrac{300}{D}$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Hence, how many days will it take 10 people to do the same job?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}D&=\frac{300}{P}\\D&=\frac{300}{10}\\D&=30\text{ days}\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: If it took 75 days to do the job, how many people were working on it?

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}P&=\frac{300}{D}\\P&=\frac{300}{75}\\P&=4\end{align*}$$There were 4 people.

teachingContext.methodNote: Part (b) explicitly assumes inverse variation. Define the variables, find the invariant product PD, and use P=300/D or D=300/P.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine the two soldier counts, use the constant soldier-days product to find the new duration, and subtract it from 20 days to answer how much less time the food lasts.

content.prompt: An army bunker currently has 60 soldiers and enough food to last them 20 days. They are joined by 40 more soldiers. Assuming inverse variation, how much less time will their food supply last?

answer.short: 8 days less; the food lasts 12 days.
answer.worked:
Let $t$ be the number of days the food lasts for 100 soldiers. The product of the number of soldiers and the duration is constant.
$$\begin{align*}100t&=60\times20\\100t&=1200\\t&=12.\end{align*}$$
The food lasts $20-12=8$ days less.

content.prompt: Let $(x_1,y_1)$ and $(x_2,y_2)$ be points satisfying the same inverse variation equation.

answer.worked:
The inverse variation equation is $y=\dfrac{k}{x}$, where $k\in\mathbb{R}$ and $k\ne0$. Since $(x_1,y_1)$ lies on it,
$$\begin{align*}y_1&=\frac{k}{x_1}\\x_1y_1&=k.\end{align*}$$

answer.short: Both products equal $k$, so dividing $x_1y_1=x_2y_2$ by $x_2y_1$ gives $\dfrac{x_1}{x_2}=\dfrac{y_2}{y_1}$.
answer.worked:
Both points satisfy the same inverse variation equation, so $x_1y_1=x_2y_2$. Since $x_2$ and $y_1$ are nonzero,
$$\begin{align*}\frac{x_1y_1}{x_2y_1}&=\frac{x_2y_2}{x_2y_1}\\\frac{x_1}{x_2}&=\frac{y_2}{y_1}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Use this formula to answer Problem 1 without needing to create a model and find the constant of proportionality: an army bunker has 60 soldiers and enough food for 20 days, and 40 more soldiers join them. Assuming inverse variation, how much less time will their food supply last?

answer.short: 8 days less; the food lasts 12 days.
answer.worked:
Use $x_1=60$, $x_2=100$ and $y_1=20$, with $y_2$ the new duration in days.
$$\begin{align*}\frac{60}{100}&=\frac{y_2}{20}\\y_2&=20\times\frac{60}{100}\\y_2&=12.\end{align*}$$
The food lasts $20-12=8$ days less.

Centre $(-5,0)$; radius $5$.

answer.worked:

answer.short:
Centre $(-3,\frac12)$; radius $4$.

content.prompt: Without sketching the following functions, categorise them as continuous or discontinuous functions over the domain $x\in\mathbb{R}$. For the functions that are discontinuous, state the value(s) of $x$ where the discontinuity has occurred.

answer.worked: The polynomial $f(x)=x^2-1$ is defined and continuous for every real $x$.
The denominator is zero at $x=0$, so $f(x)$ is undefined there. Therefore the function is discontinuous at $x=0$.
The absolute-value function is defined for every real $x$. Its two straight-line pieces meet at $(0,0)$ without a break, so it is continuous.

The inner expression $1/x$ is undefined at $x=0$. For $x\ne0$,
$$\begin{align*}f(x)&=x.\end{align*}$$
The original function still excludes $x=0$, giving a hole there. It is discontinuous at $x=0$.

Set the denominator equal to zero:
$$\begin{align*}x^2-1&=0\\(x-1)(x+1)&=0\\x&=-1\text{ or }1.\end{align*}$$
The function is undefined at these values, so it is discontinuous at $x=\pm1$.

The original denominator is zero at $x=1$. For $x\ne1$,
$$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{x-1}\\f(x)&=x+1.\end{align*}$$
Cancelling does not restore the excluded value $x=1$. There is a hole there, so the function is discontinuous at $x=1$.
For every real $x$, $x^2\ge0$, so $x^2+1\ge1$. The denominator is never zero. Therefore this rational function is continuous for all real $x$.

Set the denominator equal to zero:
$$\begin{align*}x^2+5x+4&=0\\(x+1)(x+4)&=0\\x&=-1\text{ or }-4.\end{align*}$$
For $x\ne-1,-4$,
$$\begin{align*}f(x)&=\frac{x+1}{(x+1)(x+4)}\\f(x)&=\frac{1}{x+4}.\end{align*}$$
There is a hole at $x=-1$ and an asymptotic discontinuity at $x=-4$. Both are discontinuities of the original function.

Set the denominator equal to zero:
$$\begin{align*}4x^2+4x+1&=0\\(2x+1)^2&=0\\2x+1&=0\\x&=-\frac12.\end{align*}$$
The numerator is nonzero there, so the function has an asymptotic discontinuity at $x=-\frac12$.

For continuity at $x=1$, the two formulas must agree:
$$\begin{align*}1^2+a(1)&=5(1)-2\\1+a&=3\\a&=2.\end{align*}$$

For continuity at $x=0$,
$$\begin{align*}3(0)+a&=0^2-2(0)+1\\a&=1.\end{align*}$$

For continuity at $x=1$,
$$\begin{align*}2(1)+3&=-(1)^2+a\\5&=-1+a\\a&=6.\end{align*}$$

For continuity at $x=2$,
$$\begin{align*}a(2)+2&=2a^2(2)\\2a+2&=4a^2\\2a^2-a-1&=0\\(2a+1)(a-1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Thus $a=-\frac12$ or $a=1$.

content.prompt: Recall from trigonometry the circular functions $y=\sin x$, $y=\cos x$, $y=\tan x$, $y=\operatorname{cosec}x$, $y=\sec x$, and $y=\cot x$. Which of these functions have points of discontinuity over the domain $x\in[0,2\pi]$?

answer.worked:
$\sin x$ and $\cos x$ are continuous throughout $[0,2\pi]$.

Using $\tan x=\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}$ and $\sec x=\dfrac{1}{\cos x}$, both are discontinuous at $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, where $\cos x=0$.

Using $\operatorname{cosec}x=\dfrac{1}{\sin x}$ and $\cot x=\dfrac{\cos x}{\sin x}$, both are undefined at $x=0,\pi,2\pi$, where $\sin x=0$.

Hence the four functions are $\tan x$, $\operatorname{cosec}x$, $\sec x$ and $\cot x$.

where $c$ and $s$ are non-negative integers.

If exactly 70 items are produced, $s=70-c$, so
$$\begin{align*}7c+5(70-c)&>450\\2c+350&>450\\2c&>100\\c&>50.\end{align*}$$
Thus 51–70 candles, with soaps making the total 70, meet the requirements. If fewer than 70 items are produced, both original inequalities must still hold.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate two resource limits into inequalities, find their boundary intersection, identify the common first-quadrant region, and test a production plan against both limits.

content.prompt: A manufacturer produces two types of chairs: wooden ($x$) and metal ($y$). Each wooden chair requires 3 hours of carpentry and 1 hour of painting. Each metal chair requires 2 hours of carpentry and 2 hours of painting. The factory has at most 60 hours available for carpentry and 40 hours for painting each week.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Sketch the feasible region for the production of chairs.

answer.short:
$x\geq0$, $y\geq0$, $3x+2y\leq60$ and $x+2y\leq40$. The closed feasible region has vertices $(0,0)$, $(20,0)$, $(10,15)$ and $(0,20)$.

Shade below both resource boundaries in the first quadrant. Actual chair quantities have integer coordinates.
answer.worked:
The resource constraints and non-negative quantities give
$$\begin{align*}3x+2y&\leq60&&\text{(carpentry)}\\x+2y&\leq40&&\text{(painting)}\\x&\geq0\\y&\geq0.\end{align*}$$
The boundary lines meet at
$$\begin{align*}(3x+2y)-(x+2y)&=60-40\\2x&=20\\x&=10\\10+2y&=40\\2y&=30\\y&=15.\end{align*}$$
Draw solid boundary lines. Shade the common region below both lines in the first quadrant, including the boundaries. Its vertices are $(0,0)$, $(20,0)$, $(10,15)$ and $(0,20)$. Only integer-coordinate points represent actual chair-production choices.

spec.sourceRegion: Problem 2(a); answer book PDF page 34, P2(a)
spec.description: Corrected first-quadrant feasible region. The source graph has no grid or numeric axis ticks. Blue and red distinguish the resource boundaries; light blue identifies their common feasible region.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Is it possible to make 15 wooden chairs and 20 metal chairs in one week? Justify your response.

answer.short: No. Carpentry requires 85 hours and painting requires 55 hours, exceeding the limits of 60 and 40 hours respectively.
answer.worked:
For $x=15$ and $y=20$:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Carpentry hours}&=3(15)+2(20)\\\text{Carpentry hours}&=85>60\\\text{Painting hours}&=15+2(20)\\\text{Painting hours}&=55>40.\end{align*}$$
Both resource limits are exceeded, so the production plan is not feasible.

classification.difficultyReason: Form profit by subtracting cost from revenue, recognise that the downward-opening quadratic is maximised at its vertex, and evaluate the profit there.

content.prompt: The cost of producing $x$ items is $C=2x+50$, and the revenue is $R=-x^2+60x$. Find the number of items that maximises profit, and determine the maximum profit.

answer.short:
29 items; maximum profit $\$791$.

Profit is revenue minus cost; the resulting downward-opening quadratic has its maximum at $x=29$.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}P(x)&=R-C\\P(x)&=-x^2+60x-(2x+50)\\P(x)&=-x^2+58x-50.\end{align*}$$
This quadratic opens downwards. Its vertex occurs at
$$\begin{align*}x&=-\frac{58}{2(-1)}\\x&=29.\end{align*}$$
The maximum profit is
$$\begin{align*}P(29)&=-(29)^2+58(29)-50\\P(29)&=791.\end{align*}$$
Producing 29 items gives a maximum profit of $\$791$.

content.prompt:

If $T=2$ seconds when the pendulum is 10 centimetres long, how long is a pendulum with a period of 12 seconds?

answer.worked:
Measure $T$ in seconds and $L$ in centimetres.
$$\begin{align*}2&=k\sqrt{10}\\k&=\frac{2}{\sqrt{10}}\end{align*}$$
For a period of 12 seconds:
$$\begin{align*}12&=\frac{2}{\sqrt{10}}\sqrt{L}\\\sqrt{L}&=6\sqrt{10}\\L&=(6\sqrt{10})^2\\L&=360\end{align*}$$
The pendulum is 360 cm long.

content.prompt: In physics, the gravitational force $F$ between two masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ is inversely proportional to the square of the distance $(r)$ between them. answer.short: $F=\dfrac{k}{r^2}$, where $k=12.8\text{ N}\,\text{m}^2$. Hence $F=\dfrac{12.8}{r^2}$, with $F$ in newtons and $r$ in metres. At $r=4\text{ m}$, $F=0.8\text{ N}$.
answer.worked:
For the two fixed masses, with $F$ in newtons and $r$ in metres:
$$\begin{align*}F&=\frac{k}{r^2}\\3.2&=\frac{k}{2^2}\\k&=3.2\times2^2\\k&=12.8\end{align*}$$
Thus $k=12.8\text{ N}\,\text{m}^2$ and $F=\dfrac{12.8}{r^2}$. When the masses are $4\text{ m}$ apart:
$$\begin{align*}F&=\frac{12.8}{4^2}\\F&=0.8\text{ N}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: In economics, it is assumed that demand $D$ varies inversely with price, $p$. When the price of a unit is $\$5$, $300$ units are sold. Find the demand when the price is $\$12.50$ per unit. Is the model realistic when the price becomes very small? Provide reasons for your response.

answer.short: $120$ units. The model is unrealistic at very small positive prices because it predicts demand increasing without bound, whereas real demand is limited by the number of buyers and their needs.
answer.worked:
With $p$ measured in dollars:
$$\begin{align*}D&=\frac{k}{p}\\300&=\frac{k}{5}\\k&=1500\\D&=\frac{1500}{p}\end{align*}$$
At a price of $\$12.50$ per unit:
$$\begin{align*}D&=\frac{1500}{12.50}\\D&=120\text{ units}\end{align*}$$
As the positive price approaches zero, the model predicts demand increasing without bound. Real demand is limited by the number of buyers and their needs, so the model is unrealistic for very small prices.

content.prompt: A swimmer’s time $t$ to swim 2 kilometres in the open water varies inversely with her speed $v$. Her speed $v$ also varies directly with the strength of current, $c$. She can swim the required distance in 20 minutes when $c=4$.

answer.worked:
Since $t$ varies inversely with $v$ and $v$ varies directly with $c$, $t$ varies inversely with $c$.
$$\begin{align*}t&=\frac{K}{c}\\20&=\frac{K}{4}\\K&=80\\t&=\frac{80}{c}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Justify in context whether this model is reasonable. Consider any limitations of the model.

answer.short: Reasonable only over a limited range with a following current. It ignores the swimmer’s own speed and changes in current direction.
answer.worked: A stronger following current can increase the swimmer’s speed and reduce her time, so the predicted trend can be reasonable. However, speed is not generally directly proportional to current strength: the swimmer can still move in still water. The model also ignores changing current direction and predicts unrealistically short times for extremely strong currents.

content.prompt: In astrophysics, the orbital period $T$ of a planet around a star is related to the length of the semi-major axis, $a$, of its orbit via Kepler’s third law: roughly $T^2=ka^3$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: If Earth has a semi-major axis of 2609 astronomical units (AU) and an orbital period of 365 days, find the constant of proportionality. Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}k&=\frac{T^2}{a^3}\\k&=\frac{365^2}{2609^3}\\k&\approx7.5\times10^{-6}\text{ days}^2/\text{AU}^3\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the orbital period for Saturn which has a semi-major axis of 24 900 AU. Give the period in days to the nearest 10 days, and in years to 1 decimal place. Use 365 days per year.

answer.short:
10 760 days, or 29.5 years, using the printed data.

Use the unrounded constant from part (a).
answer.worked:
Using the exact constant from part (a) and taking the positive square root:
$$\begin{align*}T&=\sqrt{\frac{365^2}{2609^3}\times24900^3}\\T&=365\left(\frac{24900}{2609}\right)^{3/2}\\T&\approx10760\text{ days}\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\text{Period in years}&=\left(\frac{24900}{2609}\right)^{3/2}\\\text{Period in years}&\approx29.5\end{align*}$$

answer.short: It assumes motion around one dominant star and neglects other gravitational influences. The constant depends on the star, and the orbit must avoid the star.
answer.worked: The model applies approximately when the star dominates the gravitational interaction. A different star generally requires a different constant. Other bodies can disturb the orbit, especially where their gravitational influence becomes significant. Very small orbits must avoid intersecting the star; weaker gravity alone does not mean that a distant orbit must stop.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires splitting absolute-value equations into sign cases, solving linear and quadratic equations, and rejecting candidates using nonnegativity or substitution; part (g) combines these routine procedures.

content.prompt: Solve the following absolute value equations for $x$.

answer.worked:
$x+5=3$ or $x+5=-3$.

$$\begin{align*}x&=3-5\\x&=-2\end{align*}$$

or

$$\begin{align*}x&=-3-5\\x&=-8\end{align*}$$

$7-2x=5$ or $7-2x=-5$.

$$\begin{align*}-2x&=-2\\x&=1\end{align*}$$

or

$$\begin{align*}-2x&=-12\\x&=6\end{align*}$$

Require $x+1\geq0$, so $x\geq-1$.

$$\begin{align*}5-3x&=x+1\\4&=4x\\x&=1\end{align*}$$

or

$$\begin{align*}5-3x&=-(x+1)\\6&=2x\\x&=3\end{align*}$$

Both satisfy the original equation.

Require $2x-5\geq0$, so $x\geq\frac52$.

$$\begin{align*}3x-4&=2x-5\\x&=-1\end{align*}$$

or

$$\begin{align*}3x-4&=-(2x-5)\\5x&=9\\x&=\frac95\end{align*}$$

Neither candidate satisfies $x\geq\frac52$. There is no solution.

Require $3-x\geq0$, so $x\leq3$.

$$\begin{align*}3x-1&=3-x\\4x&=4\\x&=1\end{align*}$$

or

$$\begin{align*}3x-1&=-(3-x)\\2x&=-2\\x&=-1\end{align*}$$

Both satisfy the original equation.

The arguments are equal or opposite.

$$\begin{align*}3x-1&=3-x\\4x&=4\\x&=1\end{align*}$$

or

$$\begin{align*}3x-1&=-(3-x)\\2x&=-2\\x&=-1\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$x=-1,7$

Split into the two possible signs and reject candidates with a negative right-hand side.
answer.worked:
Require $5x+9\geq0$, so $x\geq-\frac95$.

$$\begin{align*}x^2-5&=5x+9\\x^2-5x-14&=0\\(x-7)(x+2)&=0\end{align*}$$

The candidates are $7,-2$; reject $-2$.

$$\begin{align*}x^2-5&=-(5x+9)\\x^2+5x+4&=0\\(x+1)(x+4)&=0\end{align*}$$

The candidates are $-1,-4$; reject $-4$. Substitution confirms $x=-1,7$.

$x\neq1$.

$$\begin{align*}|x-1|&=\frac15\\x-1&=\frac15\quad\text{or}\quad x-1=-\frac15\\x&=\frac65\quad\text{or}\quad x=\frac45\end{align*}$$

Both satisfy the original equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Find the inverse-proportion constant, interpret reciprocal changes in either variable, and recognise that the three scaling results follow from a constant product for any inverse proportion.

content.prompt: Suppose that $y$ is inversely proportional to $x$ such that when $x=\frac12$, $y=4$.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the equation that relates $x$ and $y$.

answer.worked:
$y=\frac{k}{x}$.

$$\begin{align*}k&=xy\\k&=\frac12\times4\\k&=2\end{align*}$$

Hence $y=\frac2x$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If $x$ is doubled, then what is the effect on $y$?

answer.worked: Replacing $x$ by $2x$ gives $y_{\text{new}}=\frac2{2x}=\frac12\left(\frac2x\right)$. Thus $y$ is halved.

children.label: c
children.prompt: If $x$ is divided by $3$, then what is the effect on $y$?

answer.worked: Replacing $x$ by $\frac{x}{3}$ gives $y_{\text{new}}=\frac2{x/3}=3\left(\frac2x\right)$. Thus $y$ is tripled.

children.label: d
children.prompt: If $y$ is halved, then what is the effect on $x$?

answer.worked: Since $xy=2$ remains constant, halving $y$ requires doubling $x$: $(2x)(y/2)=xy$.

inlines.text: Are the results from the above three parts true in general for any quantities that are inversely proportional?

answer.worked: Yes. For inverse proportion, $xy=k$ is constant. Multiplying one quantity by a factor divides the other by the same factor.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify constant worker-hours for a fixed job, solve for workers or time, and convert the fractional hour into minutes.

content.prompt: A company can complete a job in $3$ hours with $12$ workers.

children.label: a
children.prompt: How many workers will it need to complete the same job in $2$ hours?

answer.worked:
For the same job, worker numbers and time are inversely proportional, assuming the same work rate per worker. Let $n$ be the number of workers and $t$ the time in hours.

$$\begin{align*}nt&=12\times3\\nt&=36\\n&=\frac{36}{2}\\n&=18\end{align*}$$

The company needs $18$ workers.

children.label: b
children.prompt: If the company allocates $15$ workers, how long will it take to complete the same job?

answer.worked:
The job requires $12\times3=36$ worker-hours.

$$\begin{align*}t&=\frac{36}{15}\\t&=\frac{12}{5}\text{ hours}\\t&=2\frac25\text{ hours}\end{align*}$$

The remaining $\frac25$ hour is $\frac25\times60=24$ minutes. The time is $2$ hours and $24$ minutes.

content.prompt:

children.label: a
children.prompt: How many different general ‘shapes’ can you observe forming?

answer.short: Answers vary according to how general shapes are grouped.
answer.worked: Compare graphs with coincident and distinct turning points, equal and unequal coefficient magnitudes, and both choices of sign. Reflected versions may be counted separately or grouped together, so the question does not determine a unique number.

children.label: b
children.prompt: List all the possible general shapes that you find, and state the particular values of $a$, $b$, $c$ and $d$ that resulted in each one.

answer.short: Examples: V, $|x|+|x|$; V with an extra corner on one arm, $|2x|+|x-1|$; flat-bottomed V, $|x+1|+|x-2|$; inverted V, $|x|-|2x|$; inverted V with an extra corner, $|x|-|2x-2|$; ramp between horizontal rays, $|x|-|x-1|$; horizontal line, $|x|-|x|$. Reflections give further orientations.
answer.worked:
One possible collection is shown below. The parameter order is $(a,b,c,d)$.

V: choose the plus sign and $(1,0,1,0)$.
$$f(x)=2|x|.$$

V with an extra corner on one arm: choose the plus sign and $(2,0,1,-1)$.
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}-3x+1,&x<0,\\x+1,&0\le x\le1,\\3x-1,&x>1.\end{cases}$$

Flat-bottomed V: choose the plus sign and $(1,1,1,-2)$.
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}-2x+1,&x<-1,\\3,&-1\le x\le2,\\2x-1,&x>2.\end{cases}$$

Inverted V: choose the minus sign and $(1,0,2,0)$.
$$f(x)=-|x|.$$

Inverted V with an extra corner: choose the minus sign and $(1,0,2,-2)$.
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}x-2,&x<0,\\3x-2,&0\le x\le1,\\-x+2,&x>1.\end{cases}$$

Ramp between horizontal rays: choose the minus sign and $(1,0,1,-1)$.
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}-1,&x<0,\\2x-1,&0\le x\le1,\\1,&x>1.\end{cases}$$

Horizontal line: choose the minus sign and $(1,0,1,0)$.
$$f(x)=0.$$

Replacing $x$ by $-x$ gives the reflected orientations. These examples illustrate shape families; the source does not define a unique rule for counting them.

children.prompt: For $a\ne0$ and $c\ne0$, what is the significance of $x=-\dfrac{b}{a}$ and $x=-\dfrac{d}{c}$?

answer.short: They are the zeros of the two absolute-value arguments and the possible locations of corners in the combined graph.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}ax+b&=0\\x&=-\frac{b}{a}\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}cx+d&=0\\x&=-\frac{d}{c}\end{align*}$$
Each argument changes sign at its zero. These values divide the domain into regions where the absolute-value signs can be removed consistently. Coincident changes can cancel in a difference, so a visible corner need not remain.

answer.worked: The two absolute-value terms have equal coefficient magnitudes and different zeros. Between their zeros, one term increases at the same rate as the other decreases, giving a horizontal middle section.

$$\begin{align*}x+1&=0\\x&=-1\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}x-2&=0\\x&=2\end{align*}$$

Absolute value leaves a nonnegative number unchanged and changes the sign of a negative number:

classification.difficultyReason: Students generalise from particular graphs to arbitrary coefficient magnitudes and explain why gradient cancellation occurs between the critical values for a sum and outside them for a difference.

content.prompt:
For $f(x)=|ax+b|\pm|cx+d|$, with $a
e0$ and $c
e0$, explain why there are no horizontal sections if $|a|
e|c|$. If $|a|=|c|$, explain where horizontal sections occur for the sum and for the difference. For the sum, assume the two critical $x$-coordinates are distinct.

answer.short: Branch gradients are sums or differences of $|a|$ and $|c|$, so none is zero when $|a|\ne|c|$. With equal magnitudes, the sum is horizontal between distinct critical values; the difference is horizontal outside them.
answer.worked:
Let $A=|a|$, $C=|c|$, $r=-b/a$ and $s=-d/c$. Then
$$f(x)=A|x-r|\pm C|x-s|.$$
Each linear branch has gradient of the form $\pm A\pm C$. If $A\ne C$, none of these gradients is zero.

If $A=C$, the sum has opposite contributions to its gradient between $r$ and $s$:
$$m=A-A=0.$$
It therefore has a horizontal section between distinct critical values. Its outer gradients are $-2A$ and $2A$.

For the difference, the two outer gradients are
$$m=-A+A=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad m=A-A=0.$$
The graph is horizontal to the left and right of the critical values. If the critical values coincide, the difference is zero everywhere.

entries.description:
|x − 5| = 2x − 6
x − 5 = ± ______
          = ____ or ____

Solving this, we get x = 1 or x = ____.
However, we must test to see if the solutions are valid. We can do this either by substituting or by checking the domain.

[Substituting] Substituting x = 1, we get |1 − 5| = 2 − 6, which becomes |−4| = −4, which is invalid. Hence x = 1 is not a solution.
Substituting x = ____, we get ____ = ____, which is valid/invalid (circle one).

[Checking domain] Recall that the output of an absolute value cannot be negative.
This means that if |x − 5| = 2x − 6, then 2x − 6 ≥ ____. This means that any possible solution must satisfy x ≥ ____.
Only x = ____ satisfies this, so the solution is x = ____.

entries.description: Verify your hypothesis algebraically by solving the two curves simultaneously.
entries.expectedAnswer: Subtracting the equations gives 2(x − y)² = 0, so x = y. Substitution gives 4x² = a², hence (x, y) = (a/2, a/2) or (−a/2, −a/2).

presentation.workedAnswer: Subtract the second equation from the first: 2(x − y)² = 0 ⇒ x = y. Substitute into the first: (2x)² = a² ⇒ x = ±a/2. Since y = x, the common points are (a/2, a/2) and (−a/2, −a/2). At a = 0 these coincide at the origin.

entries.description: A small business produces handmade candles and soaps. Each candle brings in $7 profit and each soap brings in $5 profit. Time constraints mean at most 70 items can be produced each week. If the profit must exceed $450, write a statement about how many candles and soaps will suit the requirements.
entries.expectedAnswer: Let c be the number of candles and s the number of soaps. The requirements are c+s≤70 and 7c+5s>450, with c and s non-negative integers. If exactly 70 items are produced, at least 51 must be candles, with the remaining items soaps.

presentation.workedAnswer: Let c and s count candles and soaps respectively. Then c+s≤70 and 7c+5s>450, where c,s are non-negative integers. If all 70 available item places are used, s=70−c, so 7c+5(70−c)>450 ⇒ 2c>100 ⇒ c>50. Thus 51–70 candles, with soaps making the total 70, meet the requirements. For smaller production totals, both original inequalities must still hold.

entries.description: In economics, it is assumed that demand D varies inversely with price, p. When the price of a unit is $5, 300 units are sold. Find the demand when the price is $12.50 per unit. Is the model realistic when the price becomes very small? Provide reasons for your response.
entries.expectedAnswer: 120 units. The model becomes unrealistic at very small positive prices because it predicts demand increasing without bound, whereas real demand is limited.

presentation.layout: Single-column standalone question; retain the explanation response with the calculation.
presentation.workedAnswer: D = k/p, so k = Dp = 300 × 5 = 1500. Thus D = 1500/p. At p = 12.50, D = 1500/12.50 = 120 units. As the positive price approaches zero, the model predicts demand increasing without bound. Real demand is limited by factors such as the number of buyers and their needs, so the model is unrealistic for very small prices.

entries.description: Discuss any limitations of this model.
entries.expectedAnswer: The same constant applies approximately to planets orbiting the same star. The model assumes the star dominates the gravitational interaction and neglects other bodies. It is unsuitable for an orbit intersecting the star or for conditions where other gravitational influences become significant.

presentation.workedAnswer: The model approximates motion around one dominant star. A different star generally requires a different constant, and other bodies can disturb an orbit. An orbit must also avoid the star; an arbitrarily small semi-major axis is not physically possible.

teachingContext.mappingRationale: Evaluates the physical assumptions and domain of a power-variation model.
